Predetermine

/pree-dih-TUR-min/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Predetermine means to decide or set something in advance, before it actually happens or before all the facts are in.

Critics accused the coach of trying to predetermine the starting lineup before tryouts had even begun.

Worked Example

The panel was supposed to review every entry fairly, but leaked emails showed the judges had predetermined the winner weeks before the contest even closed.

The judges settled on a winner before reviewing the entries — deciding an outcome in advance, before the process plays out, is exactly what predetermine means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

prearrange: to arrange beforehand

preset: to set or fix ahead of time

preordain: to decide beforehand, as if by fate or authority

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

improvise: to make something up on the spot

leave undecided: to keep a question open until later

Where it sits · how unchangeably the outcome is fixed — plan → predetermine → preordain

plan vs. predetermine: Planning sketches what you intend to do but leaves room for change; predetermining locks in the outcome itself before events even play out.

preordain vs. predetermine: Preordain is stronger than predetermine — it suggests an outcome fixed by fate or absolute authority that no one can alter.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before, in advance (Latin prae-)

Root — determine

Root — determine: to settle, decide — from Latin terminus, 'boundary, end point'

Put it together

Put it together: Pre- (before) + determine (to settle, from Latin terminus, a boundary or end point): to predetermine is to set the end point before the journey begins — the outcome is fixed and 'bounded' before events occur.

Use the root in a new word: terminate

Use the root in a new word: terminate: The company chose to terminate the contract early — to bring it to its end point ahead of schedule.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / analytical

Predetermine often carries a critical edge: calling a result 'predetermined' hints that a supposedly open process was actually settled — or rigged — in advance. The past participle is common as an adjective, as in 'a predetermined outcome.'
